findings.title: Count and fetch can observe different snapshots and exceed the row ceiling
findings.description: The count and fetch are separate statements, and the code does not establish a shared snapshot or check the fetched row count against `max_rows`. Under PostgreSQL’s default `READ COMMITTED` isolation, trades committed between those statements can make the fetch return more rows than the count admitted. The trades route has the same pattern at lines 158–164. A concurrent batch could therefore produce a response above the configured ceiling and its intended resource bound. Keep both reads on a consistent snapshot, or reject a result that exceeds the ceiling; add a test for concurrent inserts.

findings.title: Trade-filter status omits exclusions from the collection rule
findings.description: `tape_filtered()` checks only the separate trades exclusion setting. However, the trade writer also applies the general collection rule and inserts rows only when that rule selects the market and the trades filter does not exclude it (`trade_repository.py:153-173`). A market excluded by the general rule—for example, a category excluded by the default collection settings—can therefore have no collected trades while this response reports `tape_filtered: false`. With no other trade-collection status in the response, an empty result remains ambiguous. Represent the general collection-rule outcome as well, or clarify the response contract so clients are not led to interpret `false` as “not excluded from collection.”

findings.title: `tape_complete_through` is documented as the newest stored trade
findings.description: The field description says this is the “Created time of the newest stored trade,” but `tape_facts()` populates it from `sync_state.watermark_ts`. That watermark means the tape is complete through the end of the last fully walked window, not the timestamp of the newest stored trade. The OpenAPI field description should state the watermark semantics to avoid misleading API clients.
